The Potential Role
of Design
Debora B. Lombardi1 and Maria Rita Ciceri1
Abstract
Extensive evidence has documented the moderating role of design attributes
in crowding; yet, the effect of public transportation design on travel experience
has been overlooked. We conducted a within-design experimental study
aimed to estimate the buffering role of design resources in both subjective
experience (crowding, pleasantness, stimulation, and dominance) and
behavioral responses (patterns of eye movements) to crowded conditions
on a bus. Three physical bus elements (seat demarcation, access to the
window, outdoor surrounding) and their degree of supportiveness (poor,
moderate, high) were manipulated. The results of Phase 1 (N = 80) and
Phase 2 (N = 33) confirmed the beneficial moderating effect of the three
physical components on crowding and their compensatory role. The adopted
multimethodological approach confirmed to be an ecologically valid strategy
for studying the effects of the physical environment on human behavior.
Practical implications and directions for future research are discussed.
Keywords
crowding, public transportation, eye-tracking, emotional responses,
environmental design

340 Environment and Behavior 53(4)
People do not use public transit as much as they could for many reasons.
One reason for avoiding public transit is crowding. In the present study, we
discuss crowding in terms of the individuals’ perceptions of being crowded
rather than a situation in which several people are forced to stay close
together. In fact, we refer to crowding as a psychological state determined
primarily by a failure to regulate social interaction (Stokols, 1972).
Accordingly, having one person sitting too close to us might make us feel
crowded. Extensive evidence has documented the moderating role of archi-
tectural elements in the perception of crowding in several contexts of life.
What is lacking is the investigation of how the physical setting offered by
public transit could contribute to making commuting by bus or train less
aversive. Generalizing the findings from the research conducted in tradi-
tional settings, such as schools, hospitals, and residential arrangements, to
mass transit environment may be problematic, as buses, trains, and subways
represent a distinctive kind of environment with both structurally and cultur-
ally peculiar characteristics. One aim of the present study was to identify the
critical components of the physical environment offered by the public trans-
portation vehicle as well as to estimate their moderating role in alleviating
the perception of crowding and their effects on well-being. Thus, we exam-
ined the independent and buffering effects of the three components of the
mass transit physical setting on crowding (i.e., seat demarcation, window,
and the type of outdoor surrounding). Moreover, an unexplored area in the
study of crowding in general and crowding on public transportation in par-
ticular concerns the knowledge of how people visually scan a setting when
motivated to cope with overcrowding. Shedding light on the elements of a
physical setting that receives more attention may stimulate advances in the-
ory and design practice. Thus, the second aim of this study was to use eye-
tracking technology to examine where people look when in a crowded public
transport vehicle.
Crowding and Public Transportation:
Environmental Strategies to Cope With
Uncomfortable Conditions in Mass Transit Vehicle
Personal space intrusion is a primary mechanism for producing the sensation
of crowding (Evans & Wener, 2007; Walden & Forsyth, 1981; Worchel &
Teddie, 1976); yet, the only evidence of the effect of personal space intrusion
on public transportation crowding comes from a field study conducted in the
New York city metropolitan area (Evans & Wener, 2007). The study’s results
suggested that stressful reactions to seat density were due to invasions of

Lombardi and Ciceri 341
personal space rather than density per se. When people’s personal space is
violated, they try to adapt by increasing their interpersonal distance from the
intruders (Felipe & Sommer, 1966; Kaya & Erkip, 1999). However, in some
situations, such as commuting on a cramped bus, they may not be able to
adjust their interpersonal distances (Fisher & Byrne, 1975) because of social
norms (Hall, 1966; Stokols, Novaco, Stokols, & Campbell, 1978) and physi-
cal constraints (Fried & DeFazio, 1974). Consequently, passengers must find
alternative strategies to mitigate crowding.
Besides behavioral options, such as reading a book or listening to music,
architectural characteristics, including surface permeability (Evans, Lercher,
& Kofler, 2002), lighting (Leather, Pyrgas, Beale, & Lawrence, 1998), and
spatial demarcation (Evans, Lepore, & Schroeder, 1996; Evans et al., 2002),
affect perceived crowding as well as physiological and behavioral response
to crowding.
The research on the effects of the physical environment on human
responses has traditionally operationalized the physical environment con-
dition into two extreme forms: “presence” and “absence” (Evans, 1999).
However, exposure to the physical element of interest is experienced
along a continuum. A few recent studies have suggested considering the
gradient of the physical element to better quantify its effect on human
functioning (Nordh, Hartig, Hagerhall, & Fry, 2009; White et al., 2010).
In this regard, Nordh et al. (2009) adopted a sophisticated approach to
quantifying the extent to which key elements within “pocket parks” were
present, aiming to investigate variations in the perception of restoration.
They also emphasized the relevance of considering the gradient of expo-
sure to specific physical elements to inform landscape architects about
the park’s design. Likewise, we intend to consider the degree of environ-
mental supportiveness in the manipulation of each physical component.
In this study, we use the term “environmental supportiveness” to refer to
the extent to which the physical setting can support the individual’s goals
and thus improve health and well-being. Importantly, the extent of sup-
portiveness of the physical setting relies on the interplay of human char-
acteristics (e.g., specific goals and needs) and the actual social and
physical environment. For instance, partitions may foster well-being in
settings where people try to maximize their privacy (Oldham, 1988;
Robson, 2008; Tripathi, 2002); conversely, they may be detrimental when
an environment aims to encourage social interaction (Sommer, 1969).
Although the relevance of design elements in shaping crowding is well
acknowledged, empirical evidence on specific physical proprieties of
public transit and crowding has not been established.

342 Environment and Behavior 53(4)
Getting a “Good Seat” on the Bus: Demarcation,
Surface Permeability, and Visual Access to Nature
When personal space is invaded or threatened, people try to restore the social
interaction balance by better defining their spatial boundaries (Baum, Riess,
& O’Hara, 1974; Desor, 1972; Oldham, 1988; Robson, 2008). Thus, demar-
cation of spatial boundaries may decrease the probability of spatial invasion
and enhance perceived control over space (Kaya & Burgess, 2007). This is
particularly critical in the context of public transportation, where passengers
are forced to maintain inappropriate physical distances from strangers that
likely decrease their perceived control (Karlin, Katz, Epstein, & Woolfolk,
1979). Providing seats with clear boundaries on public transportation vehi-
cles may facilitate the regulation of social processes and increase perceived
control, constituting a desirable design solution to alleviate crowding.
Passenger turnover and proximity to strangers are not the only factors con-
tributing to low controllability of the mass transit travel experience. Public
transportation vehicles are by definition “movable spaces,” moving from one
geographic point to another and leaving passengers concerned about poten-
tial unpredictable events, such as unexpected traffic congestion. Thus, having
more information about time and space location may enhance a sense of con-
trol over the situation. Accordingly, the lack of perceived control is a core
aspect of commuting using public transportation (Koslowsky, Kluger, &
Reich, 1995; Wener & Evans, 2011). Therefore, establishing a connection
with the outdoor surroundings is a relevant part of the overall travel experi-
ence. Evidence regarding the beneficial effects of being visually connected to
the outside world is well established. Looking through a window provides
information about events taking place in distal surroundings, and it can pro-
vide a positive distraction (Baron, Mandel, Adams, & Griffen, 1976; Leather
et al., 1998; Ozdemir, 2010). Consistently, some evidence suggests that hav-
ing posters and pictures on the walls can reduce crowding perception and its
aversive effects (Sommer, 1974; Worchel & Teddie, 1976).
The quality of the view also modulates one’s perception. Extensive evi-
dence shows the benefits of natural views on psychological well-being and
health (Hartig, Mitchell, de Vries, & Frumkin, 2014; R. Kaplan & Kaplan,
1989). However, some authors have suggested that the healing potential is
not entirely attributable to the natural environment because even settings
constructed by humans may have potential to restore mental capacities
(Collado, Staats, Corraliza, & Hartig, 2017; Karmanov & Hamel, 2008;
Lindal & Hartig, 2013; Ouellette, Kaplan, & Kaplan, 2005).
Along with this, some evidence has supported the effect of specific physi-
cal properties of the settings, such as complexity, on the perceived restoration

Lombardi and Ciceri 343
(Abdulkarim & Nasar, 2014). Settings characterized by a high level of com-
plexity and density that fail to offer an extended view into the landscape are
perceived as unsatisfactory and overwhelming; thus, they tend to be avoided.
Traffic congestion is an example of a highly complex situation that obstructs
the view, and because of its stress, it may produce an effect equivalent to
crowding (Evans, 1999; Evans & Carrère, 1991).
Based on these findings, it is plausible to expect that the quality of the
outdoor landscape could improve the experience of public transportation and
thus reduce the perception of crowding (Hartig et al., 2014). Identifying the
types of outdoor surroundings that might affect well-being and human
responses when traveling on mass transit is another potentially significant
contribution of this study.
Measuring the Effect of the Supportive Physical
Setting of a Bus on Human Functioning: Self-
Report and Behavioral Responses
“Feeling bad” is one of the initial reactions people have when their personal
spaces have been violated (Bell, Greene, Fisher, & Baum, 2001), with an exten-
sive literature indicating that individuals develop negative mood or emotions in
crowded situations (Baum & Paulus, 1987; Evans & Cohen, 1987).
In the current work, we measured the subjective component of emotions
that are believed to have a potential buffering effect on crowding, including
pleasantness–unpleasantness, arousal–no arousal, and dominance–no domi-
nance. Previous work has demonstrated the consistency of these three emo-
tional dimensions in response to physical settings (Bradley & Lang, 1994;
Dazkir & Read, 2012; Hwang, Yoon, & Bendle, 2012; Mehrabian & Russell,
1974; Scherer, 2005).
Beyond self-report data, objective measures of people’s behavior may
help better clarify both the cause of the behavior and protective factors, facili-
tating adjustment in adverse conditions. Measures other than self-reports also
provide valuable multimethodological triangulation, enhancing the internal
validity of the research (Winkel, Saegert, & Evans, 2009). The eye-tracking
methodology has proven to be a useful strategy to supplement traditional
methods used to study human responses to specific stimuli (Berto, Massaccesi,
& Pasini, 2008; Horsley, Eliot, Knight, & Reilly, 2014; Nordh, Hagerhall, &
Holmqvist, 2013). For example, taking advantage of its capacity to unobtru-
sively analyze online cognitive processes, such as selective attention, eye-
tracking can help identify the most salient design characteristics of a physical
setting.

344 Environment and Behavior 53(4)
Tracking the Emotional Processing of a Stressful
Scene: The Contribution of Attention Patterns to
Environmental Supportiveness
Eye movements are commonly used to index cognitive processes, such as
selective attention (Parkhurst, Law, & Niebur, 2002). When we are motivated
to do something, our attention is directed toward task-relevant elements to
achieve important goals and plans (Pashler, Johnston, & Ruthruff, 2001;
Pylyshyn, 1999; Schütz, Braun, & Gegenfurtner, 2011; Tamir & Robinson,
2007; Vogt & De Houwer, 2014). Accordingly, when motivated to cope with
crowding, informative elements of the scene, such as the invader and the
physical attributes that may constitute environmental buffers, grasp our
selective attention (Vogt, De Houwer, Crombez, & Van Damme, 2013).
Gaze behavior can offer important insights into human cognitive func-
tioning in social situations (Laidlaw, Foulsham, Kuhn, & Kingstone, 2011).
When a mismatch occurs between one’s needs and environmental demands,
the presence of others may be appraised as an undesirable (social) stimulus
that would trigger coping responses and thus motivate individuals to reduce
their aversive feelings (Guerin, 1986; Laidlaw et al., 2011; Zajonc, 1965).
Laidlaw et al. (2011) found that people exhibit gaze avoidance strategies
toward strangers with whom they might engage in social interaction in real-
world situations (Laidlaw et al., 2011). Similarly, Zuckerman, Miserandino,
and Bernieri (1983) found a positive association between the use of gaze as
avoidance behavior in public spaces and experiencing crowding, such as in
the elevator.
Extensive literature on selective attention, motivation, and emotion regu-
lation (Laidlaw et al., 2011; Tamir & Robinson, 2007; Tatler, Kirtley,
Macdonald, Mitchell, & Savage, 2014; Wadlinger & Isaacowitz, 2008) sug-
gests that emotion-regulation goals direct our attention processes (Manera,
Samson, Pehrs, Lee, & Gross, 2014; Tamir & Robinson, 2007; Wadlinger &
Isaacowitz, 2011). According to Gross’s process model of emotion regulation
(Gross, 1998, 2013; Gross & Thompson, 2007), people regulate their emo-
tions toward stress-provoking social stimuli, increasing the probability of
remaining in the stressful environment rather than adopting more extreme
strategies that do not lead to habituation (e.g., flee response). To reduce nega-
tive emotions, people may use a range of strategies. For instance, reappraisal,
a powerful emotional regulation process involving the creation of an alterna-
tive interpretation of the emotional situation, often requires shifting the atten-
tion from negative elements to neutral and positive materials that are present
in the context (i.e., distraction). Thus, emotional content affects gaze pat-
terns, generating attentional biases (Calvo & Avero, 2005; Cisler & Koster,

Lombardi and Ciceri 345
2010; Koster, Crombez, Van Damme, Verschuere, & De Houwer, 2004; Xing
& Isaacowitz, 2006). As a case in point, the negativity avoidance bias involves
shifting attention away from negative stimuli to decrease negative informa-
tion in memory (Bar-Haim, Lamy, Pergamin, Bakermans-Kranenburg, & Van
Ijzendoorn, 2007; Koster et al., 2004; Mogg & Bradley, 1998; Xing &
Isaacowitz, 2006) and thus maintain positive mood (Isaacowitz, Wadlinger,
Goren, & Wilson, 2006). In one study, Xing and Isaacowitz (2006) demon-
strated that the fixation duration is shorter when people (i.e., young adults)
look at negative rather than positive stimuli. In other work conducted with a
sample from the general population, Wadlinger and Isaacowitz (2008) found
that when motivated to regulate their emotions, participants spend less time
looking at negative stimuli because of a successfully learned regulation
mechanism to avoid stressful stimulation. The body of empirical work cited
here supports the idea that attention motivation biases may serve as a marker
of emotion-regulation processing (Gross, 1998; Gross & Thompson, 2007;
Koole, 2009; Ochsner & Gross, 2005).
Besides the emotional content of the antecedent, the emotion-attention
system also depends on the qualities of the context where the scene takes
place. For instance, Vogt and De Houwer (2014) emphasized the role of an
effective distracter in successful regulation of negative emotions (i.e., dis-
gust) through avoidance biases.
Building upon the body of literature reviewed above, we propose that an
unfamiliar passenger seated next to us on the bus may represent an undesir-
able social stimulus, forcing us to deal with it. Accordingly, we would exhibit
attentional biases toward him or her. Furthermore, we would be motivated to
find buffers in the near environment that would allow us to adapt to the
adverse situation. Environmental resources of a bus coach, such as the seat
demarcation layout and the quality of outdoor surroundings, may potentially
constitute elements that can be used as buffers against crowding.
Aims and Overview of the Study
The primary aim of the study was to quantify the buffering effect of three
distinct attributes of the physical setting of a mass transit vehicle (i.e., seat
demarcation, window permeability, and quality of the outdoor surrounding)
under congested riding conditions.
Specifically, Aim 1 was to evaluate the expected role of each physical
component as a coping resource in congested rider conditions. Thus, we
hypothesized that the greatest environmental support within each physical
component (i.e., well-defined seats, high permeability of windows, and the
rural outdoor landscape) would be associated with greater positive affect and

346 Environment and Behavior 53(4)
decreased perceived crowding (Hypothesis 1a). We also hypothesized that a
change in the pattern of selective attention would indicate a positive reap-
praisal of the stressful social antecedent (Hypothesis 1b). Specifically, we
expected the greatest amount of attention toward the passenger (i.e., fixation
length and a number of fixations on AOI [area of interest] Passenger) who
represents the undesirable element in the scene (Wadlinger & Isaacowitz,
2008) when the physical environment is supportive compared with when it is
poorly arranged.
A second major aim of the study was to assess whether and how the inter-
action between the three physical attributes examined (i.e., seat demarcation,
window permeability, and outdoor surrounding) explains changes in emo-
tional responses and perceived crowding (Hypothesis 2a). We also expected
that indoor attributes of the bus setting would receive the most attention when
the outdoor surrounding is poorly supportive (Hypothesis 2b). Moreover, we
hypothesized that when the passengers’ proximal environment is the most
aversive, participants would pay selective attention to visual escapes in the
distal environment (i.e., looking out the rear window; Hypothesis 2c).
The present work included two experimental phases. Phase 1 was con-
ducted to examine subjective responses, that is, emotional responses and per-
ception of crowding, to distinct physical layout configurations on a bus to
address, at least in part, the first experimental aim. Phase 2 was run to explore
the behavioral responses, that is, gaze patterns, related to the visual scanning
of distinct physical layout configurations on a bus when one is motivated to
cope with a stressful crowded situation.
Phase 1
Method
Participants and design. Eighty students from a university in northern Italy
(35% female aged 23.71 years [SD = 3.29]) were recruited using a snowball
sampling technique and volunteered to participate in the study.
The experiment utilized a within-subjects design with 18 conditions (3 ×
2 × 3) across three factors: (a) seat demarcation: no demarcation, moderate
demarcation, physical demarcation; (b) window permeability: low permea-
bility and high permeability; and (c) outdoor surroundings: traffic conges-
tion, urban environment, rural landscape.
Materials and apparatus. Experimental stimuli included images created ad hoc
through virtual simulation (Autodesk 3DS Max ®) to systematically manipu-
late aspects of the environment while keeping all other factors constant (e.g.,

Lombardi and Ciceri 347
Figure 1. (a) Manipulation of the stressful social antecedent in the present study;
(b) illustration of areas of interest measured in the current study: (1) passenger; (2)
seat demarcation; (3) seat; (4) window; (5) rear windows.
brightness, colors, shapes, orientation). Evidence suggests that simulated
environments can validly represent actual stimuli (Bishop & Rohrmann, 2003;
Pals, Steg, Dontje, Siero, & van der Zee, 2014; Stamps, 2007).
Stimuli were created to depict a spatially uncomfortable social situation on
a bus in which one would experience crowding. Based on the classic literature
on crowding providing evidence that the presence of just one intruder who
violates one’s spatial needs is sufficient to experience crowding (Evans, 1979;
Evans & Wener, 2007; Stokols, 1972), a model of a person who occupies the
corridor seat of a double seat was added to each image (Figure 1). Images var-
ied according to the 18 conditions described above (i.e., 3 [seat demarcation] ×
2 [window permeability] × 3 [outdoor surroundings], Table 1).
To assess the effectiveness of the experimental manipulation, a sample (N
= 22; 59% female, aged 25.7 years [SD = 1.9]) of postgraduate students pre-
evaluated the experimental stimuli. Participants rated their perception of ter-
ritorial control on a 7-point Likert-type scale (i.e., Occupying this seat, to
what extent would you perceive that you could exercise control over the
boundaries of your space, 1 = absolutely disagree; 7 = extremely agree).
Similarly, it was expected that having a window with the obstructed view
versus having the seat window with a view would foster perceived openness
(i.e., Occupying this seat, to what extent would you feel you have enough
space, 1 = absolutely disagree; 7 = extremely agree) compared with the no
permeability condition. It was also expected that the quality of outdoor sur-
roundings should support restorative processes, as reviewed above. Building

Lombardi and Ciceri 349
on the Kaplan’s theorization of restorative environments (R. Kaplan &
Kaplan, 1989), we narrowed down the meaning of restoration to refer to
“being away” or (mentally) distancing from unwanted stimuli that require
cognitive effort. Such stimulus represents the restorative quality looked for in
the present outdoor surrounding. Being away distracts people from the ordi-
nary tasks involving sustained attention and thus represents the initial stage
of the restorative experience (Herzog, Black, Fountaine, & Knotts, 1997; R.
Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989). Participants rated the extent of restoration they
were likely to experience in the depicted scenes using a single item from the
Perceived Restoration Scale (i.e., Spending time here gives me a good break
from my day-to-day routine, that is, being away; Hartig et al., 1997). The
manipulation check results indicated that the experimental manipulations
were successful (see Table A1 in the appendix).
Dependent variables
Emotional reactions. Emotions are the combination of pleasure dimension,
arousal dimension, and dominance dimension in varying degrees (Mehrabian
& Russell, 1974). Using the Self-Assessment-Manikin (SAM), a nonverbal
pictorial technique to measure the aforementioned dimensions (Bradley &
Lang, 1994), participants were asked to rate a graphic character in terms of
pleasure, arousal, and dominance on a continuous 9-point scale.
Perception of crowding. Crowding was measured using a single item (i.e.,
Occupying this seat, to what extent do you feel crowded?). Participants were
asked to rate the extent to which they agreed with the given item on a 7-point
scale (from 1 = not at all, to 7 = very much).
Procedure
Participants were evaluated individually. After arriving at the laboratory, par-
ticipants signed an informed consent letter and completed some background
sociodemographic questions. Participants then received an introduction to
the simulated bus experience, “Imagine that it is early in the morning and you
are taking this bus to reach your workplace. The seat you would occupy is the
one next to the one already occupied.” They were then instructed to imagine
what their commuting experience would be like if they had to take the indi-
cated seat occupied by the depicted person as well as to look at each scene as
if they were on a real bus. Images with a resolution of 1500 × 1128 pixels
were displayed on a 19″ computer screen. The order of experimental condi-
tions was counterbalanced across participants. After each stimulus, partici-
pants were asked to rate their emotional reactions and perceived crowding.

350 Environment and Behavior 53(4)
Data Analysis
Linear mixed models (LMMs) were applied using SPSS 20. For each depen-
dent variable (i.e., pleasantness, stimulation, dominance, and perceived crowd-
ing, respectively), the main effects of seat demarcation (weak, medium, high),
window permeability (low, high), and outdoor surrounding (traffic, urban,
rural), and all interactions were included in the model as fixed factors while
participant and stimulus were initially considered random effects to control for
the variance due to differences among participants and stimuli (Gueorguieva &
Krystal, 2004; Judd, Westfall, & Kenny, 2012; McCulloch & Searle, 2001).
However, the stimulus generated a perfect matrix of identity in the estimated
models; therefore, it was excluded from further analysis. Schwarz’s Bayesian
criteria (i.e., Bayesian information criterion [BIC], Schwarz, 1978) were used
to evaluate the best fitting variance–covariance structure, which was deter-
mined to be diagonal. Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons were used to
examine interactions and main effects.
Results
The descriptive statistics for each of the variables examined in this study are
reported in Table A3 in the appendix.
Emotional reactions to the physical setting
Pleasantness. A significant main effect of seat demarcation on the rating
of pleasantness showed that participants reported greater liking in the well-
demarcated condition compared with the poorly demarcated (p < .001) while
no significant differences were found between any of the other conditions
(all p values > .133). Participants liked high window permeability compared
with low permeability. Traffic congestion was liked less compared with both
urban and rural environment with no differences between the latter two (Table
2). In addition, a significant Window Permeability × Outdoor Surrounding
interaction was found, F(2, 706.18) = 32.48, p < .001. In both low and
high permeability conditions, traffic congestion scored lower on pleasantness
compared with the natural condition (i.e., nature and low window permeabil-
ity: p < .01; nature and high window permeability: p < .001) and the urban
condition (i.e., urban and low window permeability: p < .01; urban and
high window permeability: p < .001). No differences were found between
the rural and the urban conditions by the window permeability conditions
(p > .265). All other interactions were not significant (all p values > .05).

Phase 2
Method
Participants and design. Thirty-three graduate students (males = 11, females
= 22) aged 24.86 years (SD = 3.02) enrolled in a university in northern
Italy volunteered to participate in this study. The experimental design and
the recruitment strategy are illustrated in the “Method” section of Phase 1.
Materials and apparatus. Eye movement was recorded with a remote
TOBII X120 Eye-tracker (drift < 0.3°; accuracy: 0.5°; 120 Hz) placed
under the screen monitor. The TOBII X120 Eye-tracker system allowed
for a 9-point calibration procedure. Experimental stimuli were the same as
those used in Phase 1.

Lombardi and Ciceri 355
The eye-tracking data (i.e., the overall number of fixations within each
AOI; the duration time of fixations within each AOI) were obtained using
TOBII Studio 2.0 Eye-tracker software and SPSS 20.0.
Measures
Eye movements’ metrics. To explore physical components that attract the
participants’ attention, AOIs were marked in each image. The following areas
of interest were marked (Figure 1), passenger, seat, seat demarcation, main
window, and secondary windows.
Research using eye-tracking commonly tracks eye fixations on a specific
area of the observed scene as the unit of analysis to study selective attention
(Parkhurst et al., 2002). Eye fixations are sensitive to the stimulus’ informa-
tiveness (Berto et al., 2008; Buswell, 1935) in that individuals pay more
attention to scenes that are meaningful to achieve one’s goal compared with
less informative components. The location of fixations (e.g., “How likely an
AOI is looked at?”), the number of fixations (e.g., “How much an AOI is
overall looked at?”), and the duration of fixations (e.g., “How long an AOI is
overall looked at?”) were recorded.
Procedure
The procedure was similar to the one used in Phase 1, with the addition of the
eye-tracking apparatus and individual calibration task. Each stimulus was
presented for 10 s, with each session lasting approximately 30 min.
Data Analysis
As in Phase 1, LMMs were conducted in preliminary and the main analysis
using SPSS 20. For each dependent variable (i.e., duration of fixations in
each AOI, fixations count in each AOI), the main effects of seat demarcation
(weak, medium, high), window permeability (low, high), and outdoor sur-
rounding (traffic, urban, rural), and all the interactions were included in the
model as fixed factors while participants were considered as random effects
to control for the variance due to differences among participants and stimuli.
Data analytic procedures are presented in Phase 1.
Results
Preliminary results. A preliminary analysis was conducted to verify whether a
passenger, as the undesirable stimulus, is strong enough to determine changes
in gaze behavior.

Consistent with expectations, the AOI passenger received most of the atten-
tion in terms of duration of fixations, F(4, 671.98) = 118.43, p < .001, and
number of fixations, F(4, 788.17) = 204.95, p < .001, compared with the other
AOIs examined (i.e., seat, demarcation, secondary window; all p values <
.001). Interestingly, for AOIs, the window received the same amount of eye
gaze (i.e., number of fixations; duration of fixations) as the proximate passen-

bigger size within the image (Parkhurst et al., 2002; Table A2 in the appendix)
and/or because of its salience of distraction (e.g., Worchel & Teddie, 1976).
AOI passenger. Consistent with Aim 1, the current study intended to estimate
the extent to which each physical attribute examined (i.e., seat demarcation,
window permeability, outdoor surrounding) would constitute a physical
resource to attenuate crowding. According to the results regarding the duration
of fixations on AOI passenger, a significant main effect of outdoor surround-
ing was found, F(2, 278.71) = 32.01, p < .001, revealing that individuals are
most likely to look at the passenger when the surrounding outdoor area is a
restoration-inducing landscape (i.e., rural environment) rather than an urban
landscape or a traffic congestion (p values < .001). The difference between
urban and traffic-congested surrounding scenes (p = 1.000) and the main
effects (i.e., seat demarcation, window permeability) were not significant.
Despite the absence of main effects of seat demarcation and window trans-
parency on gaze behavior, the two variables appeared to moderate the effect of
outdoor surroundings on the length with which participants looked at the pas-
senger, as demonstrated by a significant three-way Seat Demarcation × Window
Permeability × Outdoor Surrounding interaction, F(15, 53.55) = 2.22, p < .05.
In particular, when the view through the window was not obstructed (i.e., win-
dow high permeability) and the seat demarcation was either low or high, the
passenger was looked at longer when the outdoor environment was a natural
landscape rather than either the urban landscape or congested traffic conditions.
This may suggest that the passenger who was the negative actor in the scene
became less threatening when a more restorative window view was provided.
For a number of fixations on the intrusive passenger, a significant main
effect of outdoor surrounding was found, F(2, 259.01) = 11.48, p < .001,
revealing that the passenger was looked at least in the traffic congestion con-
dition while no differences emerged between urban and rural landscapes in
gazing at the passenger. No additional significant effects were observed.
The second aim (Aim 2) of the present study was to assess the efficacy of
the different design attributes (i.e., seat demarcation, window permeability, and
the quality of outdoor surrounding). Specifically, we expected that the aversive
effect of a poorly supportive design attribute would be attenuated

Lombardi and Ciceri 357
by the presence of another, more supportive design feature. Therefore, we
hypothesized (Hypothesis 2b) that when viewing a passenger who may violate
one’s personal space on the bus, wherein both well-supportive and poorly sup-
portive environmental attributes are available, people will gaze more frequently
at highly supportive elements (i.e., well-demarcated seat, permeable surfaces,
rural outdoor view) and least frequently at the poorly supportive attributes (i.e.,
poor seat demarcation, lack of window permeability, traffic congestion).
AOI seat demarcation. Consistent with Aim 2, the AOI seat demarcation was
expected to be looked at most when the outdoor environment was more stress-
ful (i.e., traffic congestion). The results revealed the main effect of outdoor
surrounding on fixations duration within the AOI seat demarcation, F(2,
205.73) = 5.97, p < .01 (Figure 3). This indicates that when the outdoor setting
was stressful (i.e., traffic congestion), participants looked significantly more at
the seat demarcation compared with the urban condition (p < .01) but not com-
pared with the rural condition (p = .423). The latter two conditions were equiv-
alent (p = .135). In addition, the main effect of window permeability on the
number of fixations within the AOI seat demarcation was significant, F(1,
341.06) = 10.65, p < .01. As expected, people were most likely to look at the
seat demarcation when the window view was obstructed compared with when
the shade was open. When the scene was obstructed partially, such as low win-
dow permeability, people tended to focus more on the elements available in the
scene. No further main effects or interactions were significant.
AOI window. The AOI window was expected to engage participants’ attention
when the interior design of the vehicle space was poorly supportive (i.e., when

was significant, suggesting that the window was looked at most when the seat

of fixations and the number of fixations on AOI window.

General Discussion
The present work set out to explore the potential of public transit design fea-
tures to ameliorate crowded interior bus conditions. Multimethodological
approaches were incorporated, including emotional reactions, perception of
crowding, and eye-tracking patterns, to assess the salience of particular physi-
cal qualities of the bus commute. To experimentally evaluate the buffering
potential of several physical attributes of the bus setting, an anticipated crowd-
ing condition on a simulated bus interior was presented to participants.
The results clearly showed that having a well-arranged seat demarcation
positively affects the quality of the users’ affective experience (see Phase 1,
Results). Interestingly, having a moderate seat boundary seems to be enough
to experience a significant positive change in perceived dominance as well as
to offset the perception of crowding. Nonetheless, moderately demarcated
seat, when compared with the poorly designed seat, was not enough to deter-
mine a significant increase in emotional well-being in terms of pleasantness
and stimulation. Thus, to help passengers feel significantly better, a stronger
barrier between seats might be required to facilitate adjustment to crowding
as well as to increase passengers’ sense of control, although it promises less
attractive experiences. We encourage future research to untangle these results.
Moreover, the findings suggest the importance of considering gradients of
protective physical attributes in public transit vehicles (e.g., the type of a
physical barrier, such as a slightly outlined partition or a well-designed

Extensive research has been conducted on the role of enclosures and physical
barriers in alleviating negative experiences with crowded conditions (Baum
et al., 1974; Baum & Valins, 1979; Desor, 1972; Evans & Lovell, 1979;
Lepore & Evans, 1996; Nicosia, Hyman, Karlin, Estein, & Aiello, 1979;
Oldham & Fried, 1987; Weinstein, 1977); yet, the effect of experiencing par-
titions of varying permeability has largely been overlooked.
Similar results were found for window permeability as well as for the type
of outdoor surrounding. Having access to the outside had a strong positive
effect on the quality of the simulated transit experience across emotional
dimensions (i.e., pleasantness, stimulation, and dominance) as well as on the
perception of crowding (see Phase 1, Results; Table 3). These results are con-
sistent with findings obtained in previous work conducted in residential and
work settings (Leather et al., 1998; McClelland & Auslander, 1978; Ozdemir,

Lombardi and Ciceri 363
2010; Ulrich, 1983; Verderber, 1986). Nevertheless, these findings did not
reveal why having a window in the immediate environment would affect the
passengers’ experience, for instance, access to the outdoor surroundings can
serve as a coping mechanism (e.g., distraction, Sommer, 1974; Worchel &
Teddie, 1976) or foster perceived control (Leather et al., 1998; Ozdemir,
2010). Because of manipulation constraints, we did not consider the gradient
for the window condition. To expand upon the current results, future efforts
could consider different levels of window permeability.
The results regarding outdoor surroundings revealed that the traffic con-
gestion significantly increased negative affect and perceived crowding,
whereas the well-designed urban scenario did not significantly differ from
the rural landscape in enhancing the quality of participants’ experience (e.g.,
Table 3). These findings are consistent with previous work on the regenera-
tive potential of urban settings (Abdulkarim & Nasar, 2014; Collado et al.,
2017; Karmanov & Hamel, 2008; Ouellette et al., 2005), which revealed that
natural and well-designed urban settings can improve the person–environ-
ment interaction (R. Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989; S. Kaplan, 1995; Ulrich,
1983), overcoming the juxtaposition between nature and human-made.
Taken together, the results of Phase 1 confirmed Hypothesis 1a. It has to
be noted that we used “being away,” one out of the four qualities of the restor-
ative environments proposed by R. Kaplan and Kaplan (1989), as the manip-
ulation check of outdoor surroundings. Although the environments that
support the experience of “being away” are also related to the high likelihood
of restoration (Lindal & Hartig, 2013), the combined effect of different
restorative qualities also increases the likelihood of restoration (Nordh et al.,
2009). Determining the components of the surrounding environment that
may facilitate other restorative processes than being away, such as fascina-
tion, and estimating their conjoint psychological effect on bus users while
experiencing crowding may provide further insights to inform practitioners
involved in environmental design. Thus, it would be highly desirable to
address this point in future studies.
In Phase 2, we proposed that the more the participants attend to the pas-
senger as a stressful antecedent of crowding, the more the physical features
will support emotional processes involved in coping with the simulated stress-
ful encounter. The results showed that only the outdoor environment plays a
significant role in determining the amount of attention spent on looking at a
nearby passenger—for example, fixations length on AOI passenger: F(2,
278.71) = 32.01, p < .001. The rural landscape appeared to provide a better
avenue for redirecting one’s attention away from the aversive situation of a
stranger sitting nearby (i.e., supporting attention deployment processes,
Ochsner & Gross, 2005; Wadlinger & Isaacowitz, 2011) and thus reappraising
